hints: State the law in its general momentum form, using the resultant force rather than beginning with the constant-mass equation F = ma.
Your statement needs to relate resultant force to the rate at which momentum changes, and it can include the direction of that change.
walkthrough: Newton’s second law links a resultant force to a change in an object’s momentum over time.
State that the resultant force is equal to the rate of change of momentum.
For a complete directional statement, add that the force acts in the direction of the change in momentum.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the resultant force is equal to, or proportional to, the rate of change of momentum.

hints: The distance travelled equals the area under the velocity–time graph because every plotted velocity from 0 to 10 s is positive.
From 0 to 10 s, the straight graph section forms a trapezium with parallel sides 9 m s⁻¹ and 13 m s⁻¹, separated by 10 s.
walkthrough: Distance travelled is the area under a velocity–time graph when the velocity stays positive, as it does from 0 to 10 s.
The graph rises linearly from 9 m s⁻¹ to 13 m s⁻¹ over 10 s, so the area is a trapezium.
Use the trapezium area: distance = ½(9 + 13) m s⁻¹ × 10 s.
This gives distance = 110 m.

ai_rubric.observable: Finds the area under the velocity–time graph, using a trapezium or an equivalent valid constant-acceleration method.

hints: Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity–time graph. Choose two clear points on the rising straight section that includes t = 10 s.
Use the points (0 s, 9 m s⁻¹) and (10 s, 13 m s⁻¹), then calculate the change in velocity divided by the change in time.
walkthrough: On a velocity–time graph, acceleration is the gradient of the graph.
From 0 s to 10 s, the velocity increases from 9 m s⁻¹ to 13 m s⁻¹.
Calculate the gradient: a = (13 − 9) m s⁻¹ / 10 s = 0.40 m s⁻².
The acceleration of the car at 10 s is 0.40 m s⁻².

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the gradient of the velocity–time graph, or an equivalent change-in-velocity-over-time calculation, for the rising section.
Obtains an acceleration of 0.40 m s⁻².

hints: Use the acceleration found in the preceding part with the car's mass of 850 kg.
Apply the resultant-force relationship F = ma using a = 0.40 m s⁻².
walkthrough: The resultant force on the car is related to its mass and acceleration by F = ma.
Use m = 850 kg and the acceleration from part (b)(ii)(1), a = 0.40 m s⁻².
The resultant force acting on the car is 340 N in the direction of its acceleration.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the 850 kg car mass with an acceleration of 0.40 m s⁻² to obtain a resultant force of 340 N.

hints: Take the direction of the car's acceleration as positive. The engine force must both overcome the two backward forces and supply the 340 N resultant force.
Add the 510 N resistive force, the 440 N tow-bar tension, and the 340 N resultant force.
walkthrough: Take the forward direction, which is the direction of the acceleration, as positive.
The engine force acts forward. The 510 N resistance and 440 N tow-bar tension act backward, while the resultant forward force is 340 N.
Therefore engine force − 510 N − 440 N = 340 N.
Rearrange: engine force = 510 N + 440 N + 340 N = 1300 N.

ai_rubric.observable: Balances the 340 N forward resultant against the 510 N resistive force and 440 N tow-bar tension to show that the engine force is 1300 N.

hints: Use the driving force found in the preceding part and the car's velocity at t = 10 s.
Mechanical power is force multiplied by velocity: use 1300 N and 13 m s⁻¹.
walkthrough: The useful output power of the engine is the rate at which its driving force does work on the moving car.
Use P = Fv with the engine force F = 1300 N and the velocity at 10 s, v = 13 m s⁻¹.
To two significant figures, the useful output power is 1.7 × 10⁴ W.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the mechanical-power relationship P = Fv.
Uses 1300 N and 13 m s⁻¹ to obtain a useful power of 1.7 × 10⁴ W.

hints: Young modulus links stress to strain. Write stress as force divided by cross-sectional area and strain as extension divided by original length.
Rearrange E = (F / A) / (ΔL / L) to make ΔL the subject before substituting the tow-bar data.
walkthrough: Young modulus is E = stress / strain = (F / A) / (ΔL / L).
Rearrange this relation for extension: E = FL / (AΔL), so ΔL = FL / (AE).
Substitute F = 480 N, L = 0.48 m, A = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² and E = 2.2 × 10¹¹ Pa.
The extension of the tow-bar is 3.5 × 10⁻⁶ m.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses Young modulus as stress divided by strain.
Expresses Young modulus using force, area, original length and extension, or rearranges the equivalent FL / (AΔL) relation.

hints: From 15 s to 17 s, the car moves towards the pedestrian at 14 m s⁻¹. Use the approaching-source form of the Doppler relation.
The 480 Hz is the observed frequency. Substitute it for fₒ and rearrange fₒ = fₛv / (v − vₛ) to find the emitted frequency fₛ.
walkthrough: The graph shows that the car travels at 14 m s⁻¹ from 15 s to 17 s. It is approaching the stationary pedestrian, so use fₒ = fₛv / (v − vₛ).
Substitute fₒ = 480 Hz, v = 340 m s⁻¹ and vₛ = 14 m s⁻¹: 480 = fₛ × 340 / (340 − 14).
Rearrange for fₛ: fₛ = 480(340 − 14) / 340 Hz.
This gives fₛ = 460 Hz, so the horn emits a frequency of 460 Hz.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the approaching-source Doppler relation with observed frequency 480 Hz, sound speed 340 m s⁻¹ and source speed 14 m s⁻¹.
Rearranges the relation to obtain an emitted frequency of 460 Hz.
